key_developments: US long-end rates became the dominant driver: flash September composite and services PMIs at 58.4 and 58.7 pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to about 5.2%, its highest since 2007, and the dollar to a two-month high on 24 September with Williams and other officials flagging further tightening after the move to 3.75–4.00%.

Five of the book's ten positions took their entire weekly gain from the 23 and 24 September sessions: GBP/USD to 1.32200, NZD/USD to 0.56619, AUD/USD to 0.70122, USD/CAD to 1.41413 and USD/CHF to 0.82854.

The SNB held at 0% on 24 September, raised its inflation forecast for every year to 2028 and returned to standard FX-intervention wording; SGD/CHF closed 25 September at a cycle high 0.64853, through both its tactical and strategic objectives.

RBNZ October hike pricing ran from about 20% earlier in the month to roughly 87% (a separate read at 75%) after Governor Breman warned sustained oil gains could push near-term inflation above projections.

Australian unemployment rose to 4.6% against an expected 4.5% on 24 September with 39,500 jobs added and participation at 67.1%; futures moved to roughly 90–94% for a 29 September RBA hike with all seven major banks forecasting one.
Singapore August CPI on 23 September printed headline 2.3% and core 2.2%, firm but read as supporting a hold at the 14 October MAS review; USD/SGD closed 1.28021 that day.
GBP/JPY closed 208.36845 on 25 September, below the 209.42 threshold on session five of the ten-session post-BoJ clock, defusing the book's only armed dated invalidator.
UK fiscal stress deepened without a new event: the 30-year gilt yield reached 5.90% on 25 September and sterling fell anyway, confirming the terms-of-trade channel over the rate channel.
new_risks_identified: US and Iranian negotiators are reportedly exploring a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz; Brent peaked just above $108 intraday and closed $106.6 on Thursday. A de-escalation removes the energy premium under the sterling terms-of-trade thesis, the BoE's November hike case and the RBNZ's hawkish pivot simultaneously.
A US 10-year near 5.2% has become the dominant input for six of the ten tracked positions regardless of their local stories — a term-premium mechanism the original analysis did not model.
The 5 November BoE decision at 69–81% implied now sits inside the file window and is named in invalidators for EUR/GBP and GBP/JPY while touching four sterling positions at once.

The New Zealand rate curve has turned against two kiwi shorts and Long AUD/NZD that are all far beyond any published exit level, with the 28 October RBNZ Monetary Policy Review now a live hike rather than a formality.

EUR/GBP: consensus has turned hawkish on both legs — 75.1% October / 73.3% December for the ECB and MUFG anticipating 50bp of BoE tightening from November — the one configuration the trade cannot easily survive.

NZD/USD and NZD/JPY: rate consensus has moved decisively against the shorts (October RBNZ at ~87% versus 20% earlier in the month) while spot has moved decisively toward them, leaving spot roughly 335 pips below the 0.60 bank cluster centre.
